1:
The date is agreed; the almanac is not. Gill notes that some make the third year the last of the reign, but that by an old canon and by Josephus the king reigned seventeen years; and he lists four attempts at the year, two placing it in 553 before Christ, another in 552, and a fourth, which he calls very wrong, in 537, two years after the king was dead. Henry takes the third year to have proved the last, so that this chapter should stand in order of time before the fifth, and Gill likewise puts this vision before what the two following chapters record. Ellicott says only that it was most probably not long before the end of the reign. Gill and Ellicott both mark the change of language, Gill saying that having related what concerned the Chaldeans the prophet had written in Chaldee, and now, writing of things that concerned the Jews and the church of God in later times, he writes in Hebrew; Ellicott says the same from the other side, that the Chaldee is dropped because the visions in the rest of the book have no connection with Babylon.

What the vision is for is answered at three scales. Keil and Delitzsch describe the whole part: it contains three revelations received under three kings, and where the first part of the book described the development of the world-power, this second part reveals how the kingdom of God, at war with the rulers of the world and amid severe oppressions, is carried forward to final victory; the first of the three shows what will happen to the people of God during the second and third world-kingdoms. Wesley says the same in a line, that the earlier vision spoke of all four monarchies and this only of the first three, being a comment upon the first. Calvin adds the pastoral reason: God had shown the four monarchies lest the faithful should grow weary at seeing the world so often convulsed and suppose themselves rejected by him; here he shows one part only, since the fall of Babylon was at hand.

Whom the vision points to is the chapter’s great division. Calvin says the chief object of the vision is to prepare the faithful to bear patiently the horrible tyranny of Antiochus, and reads the whole as leading, through the second redemption which was the second birth of the Church, to the coming of Christ, since God then afforded only a taste of true redemption. Clarke reports the same identification and declines it: the little horn is supposed by some to denote Antiochus Epiphanes, but seems to him to apply more properly to the Roman power in general, by which the polity and temple of the Jews were destroyed.

Whether the prophet was really at Shushan divides them. Clarke says he was: Shushan appears to have been a strong place where the kings of Persia had their summer residence, the capital of the province of Elam, most probably added to the Chaldean territories by Nebuchadnezzar, and it was Daniel’s ordinary residence, so that being there he saw himself in vision on the banks of the Ulai, the same as the river Euleus. Ellicott says flatly that he was at Susa only in vision and was not bodily transported thither, and Henry likewise says he was not there in person. Calvin argues the point: the word vision is added to show that the ram was not seen by the eyes of the body but was a heavenly oracle, raising the beholder above all human sensations; and as for those who think the prophet then dwelt in Persia, who could persuade a captive attached to the king of Babylon to depart as though his own master and go into Persia while the Persians were open enemies? Calvin says he wonders what can induce men to adopt so unreasonable a comment.
3:
Why the empire is a ram Calvin asks most directly. It ought not to seem absurd, he says, that God proposed various similitudes, since the prophet had to teach a rude people in various ways; and he does not think we need inquire scrupulously why the Persian kings are called rams, knowing no valid reason unless it be to institute a comparison with Alexander and his successors. On that supposition the image does not illustrate the Persian empire absolutely, but only by comparison with the Macedonian. The best reason he finds in the humble origin of the Persian kings: Cyrus is fitly a ram, since his horn produced a concussion through the whole earth when no one expected anything to spring from a region by no means abounding in anything noble; and Alexander is a he-goat, far more nimble and yet more obscure in his origin, for what was Macedon but a mere corner of Greece? Clarke answers from the monuments instead: a ram was the symbol of the Persians, and a ram’s head with two horns, one higher than the other, appears in various parts of the ruins of Persepolis.

What the beast stands for is put two ways. Clarke says the ram points out the empire of the Medes and Persians and particularly Cyrus its founder, son of the king of Persia and grandson of the king of Media, who by marrying his uncle’s only child succeeded to both crowns. Keil and Delitzsch make the corresponding point about the goat, that it represents not the person of the king but the kingship, since the great horn between its eyes symbolises the first king and the goat therefore cannot itself be a separate king; it comes from the west because Macedonia lay west of Persia. Clarke also explains the order of the horns: Media, the shorter, was the more ancient kingdom, while Persia, the higher, had come up lately and was of little consequence until Cyrus, after which it far outstripped anything Media had been.

The three directions are filled in by name. Gill lists the west as Babylon and Syria and part of Greece, the north as Armenia and Scythia and Colchis and the shores of the Caspian, and the south as Arabia and Ethiopia and Egypt and India; Wesley gives nearly the same, adding Cappadocia and the Lydians. Clarke reduces it to three theatres, the Scythians northward, the Greeks westward and the Egyptians southward, and observes that no other nation at that time could stay the progress of the Persian arms. Why the east is left out gets two answers: Gill says the ram stood in the east facing westward, so that north and south lay to his right and left, while Ellicott says he does not push eastward because he is presumed to have made his conquests there already; Ellicott adds that the three directions answer to the three ribs in the mouth of the bear.

Calvin extends the verse past Cyrus and pauses over the histories. The prophecy takes in all who came after him and convulsed the whole world; Cyrus himself, according to many historians, was shortly afterwards cruelly and basely slain, though one excellent writer affirms that he died in his bed. Calvin warns against trusting that writer here, since under the image of the king he wished to set before us an example of perfect manliness, bringing him forward on his deathbed exhorting his sons to kingly virtues; whichever account is true, Cyrus was overtaken in the midst of his career, and by this God chastised an insatiable cupidity in which he resembled Alexander. As for the successors, they raised such commotion as to stir up heaven and earth, one boasting that he could bind the sea with fetters; and their pride left no end to their warfare till they had subdued the distant boundaries of the world.
5:
Why a goat stands for Macedonia Clarke answers from the name. Two hundred years before this prophet, he says, the Macedonians were called the goats’ people, from a story that their first king, seeking a new habitation, was advised by an oracle to take goats for his guides, and, seeing a herd flying from a storm, followed them to the place where he fixed his seat, made the goats his ensigns, and named both town and people after them; and Alexander called his son by Roxana the goat. Ellicott finds the propriety in the contrast rather than the etymology, the goat and the ram forming the same opposition as the panther and the bear, activity against strength and brutal fierceness. Wesley says simply that the goat is the Grecian empire and the horn Alexander.

The speed of the conquest is what all dwell on. Clarke says the goat seemed to fly from conquest to conquest, and that by the time Alexander was thirty he had conquered all Asia, which is why the earlier vision gives him four wings. Ellicott calls the not touching of the ground an exact prediction of those conquests, all his movements being characterised by marvellous rapidity, and notes that from the first battle to the last only three years elapsed. Calvin says the same of the swiftness, that he rather flew than travelled, and that a man galloping through regions completely at peace could not have passed through Asia more speedily. But Calvin reads the phrase about the face of the whole earth differently: Alexander’s arrival in Asia with a very insignificant army is well known, since he thought thirty thousand men sufficient once the states of Greece had made him general, so the words mean not numbers but the terror inspired on every side.

The onset itself is told with relish. Gill has Alexander, chosen captain general of all Greece, pass the Hellespont and come up to a king at the head of a numerous army, adding that though many rivers and mountains lay in the way which seemed impassable, he got over them all. Clarke names the fields: the Persian generals were first vanquished at a river in Phrygia, then the king himself routed at a strait in Cilicia and afterwards on a plain in Assyria; and one can hardly read the words, he says, without seeing the Persian army guarding that river and Alexander on the other side plunging in and swimming across and rushing on the enemy with all the fire and fury that can be conceived. Calvin counts differently, saying Darius was conquered in two battles, after which the Persian sway throughout Asia Minor was completely ruined, and that though an immense multitude had been collected the preparation was available for nothing but empty pomp.

Calvin alone treats the fury as a fault. Darius was fortified both by the distance of his stations and the strength of his fortifications, many of his cities reckoned impregnable, so that it was incredible the he-goat should ever come near the ram. Yet we are well acquainted with the keenness of Alexander’s talents and the superiority of his valour, Calvin says, and such was his unbridled audacity that his promptness approached rather to rashness than to regal bravery, since he often threw himself with a blind impulse against his foes, and it was not his fault if the Macedonian name was not destroyed ten times over. Clarke gives a plainer motive: the Persian king had tried to draw off his captains with bribes and to procure his assassination, after which Alexander would listen to no proposals of peace; Persepolis was sacked and the whole monarchy overturned. Keil and Delitzsch pass to the sequel: by the kingdom of the ram the he-goat became very great, but the great horn was broken at the height of his strength and four grew up conspicuously in its place.
8:
The breaking of the great horn is dated and explained. Clarke says Alexander died in the height of his conquests at about thirty-three, that his brother and his two sons kept up the name of the Macedonian kingdom for a time but were all murdered within fifteen years, so that the great horn was broken and the family cut off. Wesley puts it most sharply: when Alexander was greatest then was he broken to pieces, since he and his mother and son and brother and all his kindred were destroyed. Calvin observes that the great horn means the monarchy which was solely in Alexander’s power while he lived, since he was the first and last monarch of his race, and that because his generals afterwards became kings the he-goat is not restricted to his person but extends to his successors. Calvin adds that how he died is unknown, whether by disease or poison, since the historians report a great suspicion of foul play, and that the angel notices not his age but those successes, gained at the constant hazard of his life by a man of far more audacity than skill.

The four kingdoms are named, and no two lists agree. Clarke says the provincial governors usurped the title of kings and, one being slain in battle, were reduced to four: Seleucus with Syria and Babylon in the east, Lysimachus with Asia Minor in the north, Ptolemy with Egypt in the south, and Cassander with Greece in the west. Wesley gives Greece to Antipater, Asia to Antigonus, Egypt to Ptolemy and Babylon with Syria to Seleucus. Ellicott offers two possibilities rather than a list: the four horns may mean the dispersal of the empire to the four winds at its founder’s death, or may hint at its division into four parts, Thrace and Macedonia beside Syria and Egypt. Gill leaves the succession alone and marks the man instead, that Alexander was very great in his own esteem, reckoned himself lord of the world and affected to be worshipped as a god.

Who the little horn is divides the chapter. Gill sets aside two readings by name, the kingdom of Titus Vespasian and the kingdom of the Turks, and takes it for Antiochus Epiphanes, who sprang from the Seleucidae in Syria, that is from one of the four horns. Wesley says the same without argument, and Ellicott with references, pointing to the southern campaigns and eastern wars of Antiochus. Clarke reports the identification and prefers another: some think Antiochus is meant, but he follows a bishop who makes it the Roman government, very great at its zenith and yet very little in its rising. On that reading the growth toward the south is Egypt made a province, toward the east the conquest of Syria, and toward the pleasant land the taking of Judea, followed by the burning of the city and temple.

The pleasant land is agreed; the grammar is not. Ellicott takes it for Palestine, a third land lying between the south and the east, and says the phrase was suggested by earlier prophets; Wesley says it is called pleasant because of the temple and the people of God in it and its fruitfulness. Keil and Delitzsch spend their note on the words that introduce the horn: the word one after horn is a numeral, meaning one horn and not several, and the particle before the word for little is taken by some as comparative, less than little, by others as less than insignificance, which they call untenable, preferring a circumlocution for the superlative. Calvin explains why the warning was given at all: nothing torments men more than being bewildered in false imaginations and thinking the world the sport of chance, so God taught the pious beforehand the nature of their afflictions, that they might know these scourges proceeded from him and not glide downwards into despair.
10:
Who the host of heaven are is the first dispute. Clarke takes the host for the Jewish hierarchy and the stars for the priests and Levites, and thinks the same phrase is used by our Lord for that hierarchy. Keil and Delitzsch begin from the letter, that the host of heaven is the whole body of the stars: the prophet sees the horn grow so great in height that it reaches the heavens and can lay hold of the heavenly bodies with the hand, throwing some down to the earth and trampling on them in scorn. But the angel’s words further on show that by the stars we are to understand the people of the saints; so the stars cast down are neither the Levites nor the illustrious men of Israel, both of which readings they set aside. Gill and Wesley agree, Gill calling them the church militant whose names are written in heaven, Wesley adding that among them the priests and champions were as stars shining above the rest.

Calvin turns the figure into consolation. Without the slightest doubt it marks the elect people of God; and although the Church often lies prostrate in the world, trodden under foot and buried, it is always precious before him. The prophet adorns it with this praise, not to obtain honour for it before men, but because God has separated it from the world and provided a sure inheritance in heaven; for though the sons of God are pilgrims on earth and like castaways before men, they are citizens of heaven. The teaching, Calvin says, induces us to bear it patiently when we are thrown prostrate and despisers of God look down on us with scorn: our seat is laid up in heaven and God numbers us among the stars, although, as Paul says, we are as the offscouring of all things.

Who the prince of the host is gets three candidates. Gill names the high priest Onias, whom the king put out of his office, or Judas Maccabeus as prince of the Jewish nation, or rather, as he prefers, God himself, whom Antiochus blasphemed, whose worship he stopped and whose temple he profaned. Wesley says the offence was against God himself as well as the high priest. Keil and Delitzsch reject the priestly reading outright: the prince of the host is not the high priest but the God of heaven and King of Israel, the Prince of princes. Calvin refuses it in the same terms, that some take the prince of the army for the high priest, since priests are sometimes so called, but that this is too forced; the true sense imputes such arrogance to Antiochus as to urge him to declare war with the stars of heaven, implying not only opposition to the Church but a daring defiance of God himself. Ellicott says simply that it is Jehovah.

The last clauses are glossed briefly. The words are horrible in their import, Calvin says, for God was thus spoiled of his rights, having chosen but a single corner of the world for his special worship; and what heathen would not despise such forbearance, in permitting himself to be deprived of his honour by so sordid a tyrant, skilful only in cunning and the basest flattery? On the taking away of the daily sacrifice Ellicott glosses the word as everything permanent in the worship of God, while Wesley says the use of the temple was taken away as to the holy service. Clarke refers it instead to the destruction of the city and temple, never restored from that day to this. Keil and Delitzsch add a caution: this verse does not record a part of the vision but is a further development of it in prophetic words, so its contents may not be referred to heavenly events, as though a heavenly sanctuary were destroyed.
12:
This verse is the most contested in the chapter, as Keil and Delitzsch say: its first half has been very variously interpreted. Gill sets out four readings before choosing. Some take the host given him for a garrison placed by Antiochus to hinder the daily sacrifice; others for a host of apostates among the Jews who advised him against it, and to kill swine and offer them on the altar; or the words may rather be rendered that the host was given over to the enemy because of the transgression against the daily sacrifice, so that for the neglect of it by priests or people the Jews were delivered into his hand. Gill adds a fourth, that two Jewish interpreters take the word for a set time which shall have an end, and reports that Calvin inclines to that sense.

Calvin does, and gives his reason. The word signifies both army and time, but the latter is the more suitable, since when it is translated that an army shall be given him the sense appears forced; Calvin more willingly embraces the sense of a time allowed, that God will try the patience of his Church for a definite period and then bring their troubles to an end. It is impossible, he says, to sustain the spirits of the faithful otherwise than by their expectation of a favourable termination, and this is why God shows the temporary duration of the sway of Antiochus: whatever the tyrant may intend, he shall not abolish the worship of God, since God will not permit the sacrifices to perish for ever, but will restore them.

Keil and Delitzsch reject exactly that rendering, and the older one behind it. The Latin version gives that strength was granted against the daily sacrifice on account of sins, and a well-known later translation follows it; the other rendering, that a time was given over the daily sacrifice, follows an older Jewish commentator, taking the word first for a military station and deriving from that the sense of time. Both must be set aside, they say, since the word means neither strength nor time nor a military station, but only military service and perhaps military forces; and besides, the same word in the verses immediately before and after plainly means host. If that is maintained, only two explanations remain, according as the host is understood of Israel or of some other host.

Those who take it for the Jewish people divide over what was given. Ellicott holds the host to be the same as the one mentioned earlier and to mean some of the Jewish people, since some lapsed under the persecutions of Antiochus and joined in his idolatrous rites; these apostates were given into his hand, and on account of their apostasy the daily sacrifice was taken away. Wesley marks the transgression as belonging both to the priests and to the people. Clarke takes the host for power, or perhaps for the priesthood and the whole sacrificial system, and refers the whole to a later ruin: they had filled up the measure of their iniquities in rejecting the Lord that bought them, and the daily sacrifice, being no longer of use, was given up with the rest to destruction.

Why God allowed it at all is Calvin’s opening question. It seems absurd that such licence should be given to Antiochus, that the temple should be spoiled and all worship exterminated; and the difficulty is real, since the opinion will creep in that God is perhaps constrained and unable to subdue his foes. The prophet therefore states plainly that the licence to vex the Church would never have been granted without God’s permission: the pious have no cause for desponding while they see all things confused, since God rules these perplexities by his secret judgment, and Antiochus can do nothing by his unbridled audacity unless divinely permitted and previously limited.
13:
Who the speakers are is quickly settled. Clarke says one angel asked another how long the sanctuary was to be trodden down; Wesley puts the question in his own words, how long shall Antiochus continue his vexations and prevent the worship of God. Ellicott notes that only a portion of what the angels said is set down, and glosses the question as asking how long the object of the vision shall last so far as it has to do with the great apostasy. Calvin explains why an angel asks at all: the prophet was so overcome by fear as scarcely to dare to inquire, and God, providing for his infirmity, interposed and sent an angel to make the inquiry in his name, which Calvin calls no common proof of paternal goodness.

Keil and Delitzsch use the verse to settle an earlier word. The construction here, they say, is derived not so much from the words of the text as from a reference to the history, since it is supposed that because the wickedness of Antiochus is in question the entrance of the Syrian army into Jerusalem must be what is set forth. But the word for host cannot properly be understood in the earlier verse otherwise than here, not of the host of the Syrians but only of the people of Israel. Calvin, for his part, takes the treading down concretely: the very spot which God had promised should be his perpetual dwelling-place was exposed to impious superstitions, since the idol of Jupiter Olympius was set up there, as the history of the Maccabees relates.

Who answers, and to whom, is Calvin’s next question. The reply belongs not to the angel who inquired but to the Wonderful One, from which Calvin gathers the great anxiety of the angel about the interpretation, not for his own sake but for the common benefit of the pious. Of that Wonderful One he is persuaded it was the Son of God, but says that whoever he was he does not reject the angel’s request; the answer goes to Daniel rather than to the angel because the angel had taken up the cause of the whole Church rather than his own. Gill says the same, that the answer was given to Daniel who stood by, since the questioner knew it was for his sake and his people’s that the question was asked.

The number is where the chapter divides again. Calvin insists on plain days: the Hebrews are at variance whether years or months are meant, but it is surprising how grossly they are deluded in so plain a matter, since the expression can be used of neither, and we ought evidently to understand natural days of twenty-four hours; those who take it of years and months are wretchedly mistaken and even ridiculous in their calculations, some beginning from Samuel and descending to the reigns of Saul and David. Wesley agrees in effect, reckoning the term from the defection of the people procured by a high priest to the cleansing of the sanctuary. Ellicott reckons the same way and works it out: the period ends with the cleansing and begins with the transgression that led to the events under Antiochus, and though the dates are not recorded precisely, two thousand three hundred complete days make six years and a hundred and forty days. That falls short of seven years by about two-thirds of a year; and if seven be the number symbolical of divine chastisements, the prophecy implies that the people shall not suffer according to their full deserts, but that for the elect’s sake those days shall be shortened. Clarke takes the opposite view, that the prophetic day is meant here as elsewhere in this prophet and must signify so many years, and reckons from the invasion of Asia by Alexander to a date more than a century after his own.
15:
Gill takes the repeated name as a defence of the vision itself: the prophet repeats the affirmation and gives his own name, partly for emphasis and partly for greater confirmation. Gill calls it a most impudent thing in Porphyry to say that the true Daniel never saw this vision, but that it was written after the reign of Antiochus and falsely ascribed to him; the prophecy being so clear concerning Alexander and the destruction of the Persian empire, that spiteful heathen had no other way of evading it. Henry marks what he did with it: those who rightly know the things of God cannot but desire to know more, and must seek the meaning diligently; the prophet compared the vision with the former discoveries, but especially he sought by prayer, and did not seek in vain.

Who the man-like figure is divides them. Clarke says the appearance of a man is supposed to be the Messiah, while Wesley calls the figure probably Gabriel but still assigns the voice to Christ. Ellicott separates the two the other way: the figure was Gabriel, while the voice proceeded from him who alone has authority to command angels. Henry puts it as a question, that one in the appearance of a man, whom some think was Christ, gave the order, for who else could command angels? Calvin treats no longer of a man or a figure but of a voice, and Scripture often records that angels appeared as men and are called indiscriminately either angels or men; the same person is meant as before, because he commands the angel, which can be referred to Christ alone. The name Gabriel, the strength of God, suits the case; but here the angel receives his commands from Christ, so that supreme authority is represented under the form of a man and obedience portrayed in Gabriel; and from this the divinity of Christ is inferred, since he could not issue orders to angels without being God himself.

Why the prophet fell down is agreed and why he was called son of man is not. Keil and Delitzsch say he fell in terror because as a sinful and mortal man he could not bear the holiness of God appearing in a pure heavenly being, and feared he must die. On the address that follows they take issue with the obvious reading: son of man stands against the name of Gabriel, man of God, and reminds the prophet of his human weakness, not in order to humble him, for which there was no occasion, but to inform him that he was notwithstanding deemed worthy of high divine revelations. Wesley takes exactly the reading they refuse, that he is called son of man to make him mind his frailty and not be lifted up by so great a condescension.

The time of the end is left open. Clarke reports another rendering, that the vision shall end at the proper time. Ellicott allows two senses, the final period of earthly history or the time at the limit of the prophetic horizon, and cites Jerome for the view that what happened under Antiochus was typical of what shall be fulfilled hereafter. Wesley says it means God’s appointed time in the latter day, not in the prophet’s own lifetime. Calvin closes on the reverence rather than the date. This awe was always present whenever he perceived himself taught by God, but here a special feeling is expressed, since God desired to influence his mind so as to set us an example and make us more attentive, using the angel as his servant while inwardly touching the prophet by his Spirit. Calvin adds that if an unbeliever entering the assembly and hearing a prophet speak in God’s name would fall on his face, how great will our troubles be unless we receive most reverently what we know was uttered by the mouth of God.
18:
The prophet is found on his face and set on his feet again. Ellicott notes only the effect of heavenly visions upon those who beheld them, and Wesley says he was toward the ground because he was terrified with the splendour and grandeur both of the messenger and the message; he was set upright by one touch only, the power of spirits being incomparably greater than that of the strongest of men. Calvin makes the repetition deliberate. The prophet says again how he was frightened by the magnitude of the vision and how he was raised up by the angel, lest he should remain in that stupor; two clauses are to be noticed, that he was astonished at the outset, for he could not otherwise have been composed enough to listen, and that the angel set him upright in his place.

From those two clauses Calvin draws the rule. Whenever God addresses us we must be subject to fear and dread, since that produces humility and renders us docile, and fear is the true preparation for obedience. But another feeling ought to follow, for God, having prostrated us, will also raise us up; and that disposition cannot arise unless our minds are sedate. Readers ought therefore to collect all their senses, conscious that they are unable to understand anything unless the fear of God goes before.

The angel then states what he has come to do. Gill takes the words to mean that he will make known to the prophet what he knew not, even things future. Ellicott reads the end of the indignation as the revelation of the wrath of God at the end of the time of the prophecy, and the time appointed as saying that the vision refers to the appointed time in the end. Wesley puts a name to the indignation: God will raise up Antiochus to execute his wrath against the Jews for their sins, yet there shall be an end of that indignation.

Calvin argues over the words rather than the sense. Those who read the noun in the genitive in the preceding verse understand the word vision again here, as though it ran, at the time of the end there shall be a vision; but since the word signifies a time fixed and settled beforehand, there is nothing superfluous in the plainer method of speech, and the other would be harsh and far-fetched. All agree as to the matter, since the angel bears witness that he is the interpreter chosen by God.

What Calvin makes of that witness is a caution about authority. The angel here acquires confidence from his office, having accepted the commands divinely laid upon him, and this ought to be remarked, since our faith will never rest or become firm unless the authority on which it is founded be fixed. Ought we then to put confidence in men who conduct themselves with rashness and assume authority in the name of God without a certain and lawful calling? Neither angels nor men are to be held in such honour as to induce us to receive whatever they bring forward, unless God has appointed them his ministers and interpreters. By the phrase itself, Calvin adds, the angel asserts the suddenness of the wrath of God.
20:
The angel begins the particular explanation, and Gill marks it as such: the first thing the prophet saw, a ram with two horns, is now named. Keil and Delitzsch take the two horns for the kings of Media and Persia and draw a large conclusion from the naming. Since the vision relates to the Medo-Persian and the Javanic world-kingdoms, and to the persecuting kingdom of Antiochus which arose out of the latter, it cannot be disputed that here, in prophetic perspective, the time of the end is seen together with the period of the oppression of the people of God, and the first appearance of the Messiah together with his return in glory to the final judgment. They then take up an objection that the intimate causal connection between the coming of the Messiah and the end of all things does not make the two contemporaneous, but their block breaks off before the answer is given.

Calvin explains how one ram carried two horns. Two kingdoms coalesced in one: Cyrus granted it for a time to his father-in-law Cyaxares but drew the whole power to himself, and the Persians began to extend their sway over all the East; God in this vision had respect to the beginning of that monarchy, and when the Persians and Medes were united the ram bore two horns.

The goat follows. Gill reads the rough goat as the kingdom of Greece, which began in Alexander and continued until it was destroyed by the Romans, and finds the figure fitted to him for his strength and prowess, his swiftness in marching over rocks and mountains, and his majesty and grandeur. Calvin adds a note on the name: by Javan the Hebrews designate not only the Greeks but the Macedonians, and the whole tract which is divided by the Hellespont from Asia Minor, so that the meaning is simply the king of Greece.

Then the great horn is broken. Gill notes that the death of Alexander, either by drunkenness or by poison, is what the breaking expresses; Calvin says he perished in the flower of his age, scarcely thirty years old, and that great suspicion of fraud attaches to the manner of it. On the four that stood up in his place Calvin contests a rendering. Some skilled in the Hebrew translate that they arose from the nations, which changes the number and misses the intention of the angel, who is confirming the unity of the kingdom and its division into four parts: they sprang from a single origin. By what right did Ptolemy obtain the empire, except by being one of the generals of Alexander? At the beginning he dared not use the royal name nor wear the diadem. Cassander the son of Antipater obtained Macedon, Ptolemy Egypt, and Antigonus his own fourth share.

The last clause limits them all. Clarke says the four kingdoms shall not be of the power or family of Alexander, nor have his strength and dignity; Ellicott glosses it briefly, not like the first king. Calvin makes the same point from the size of the horns, which are so small that not one of them should be equal to the first king, since Alexander had touched upon the Indian sea and enjoyed the tranquil possession of his empire throughout the whole East, having filled all men with the fear of his industry, valour and speed.

Calvin will not leave the prophecy as history. He asks how the prophet could conjecture events so long before they happened, when he does not pronounce mere enigmas but narrates things exactly as if they were already fulfilled: the ram had not yet risen and seized upon Babylon, and Philip, a most skilful warrior who surpassed all the kings of Macedon for cleverness, never dared to cross the sea or attack the power of Persia.
23:
When the latter time falls is disputed only in degree. Gill sets it toward the close of the four kingdoms, when the Grecian empire was decreasing and coming into the hands of the Romans, and King Antiochus rose up. Wesley says it is when they were come to the height and beginning to decline. Calvin guards the phrase against being pressed: it does not imply that the four kingdoms had ceased, for the successors of Antiochus were not directly cast down, Perseus was the last king of Macedon, and the Ptolemies continued to the times of Julius Caesar and Augustus; the angel means only that their final ruin was at hand and their royal majesty already fleeting, since they depended upon the Romans.

Who the transgressors are is asked next. Ellicott takes them for the apostate Jews, who have filled up the measure of their guilt so as to exceed the limits of mercy. Wesley says the Jews were grown to an excess of wickedness, and then God suffered Antiochus to persecute them. Calvin knows of an opinion that applies the word to the professed and outward enemies of the Church, but prefers the reading that finds the impious within: after the prophets had treated so fully of the happy state of the people restored from captivity, to behold the horrible dispersion and tyrants assaulting the temple itself was no common temptation, and the angel fortifies the prophet by showing that God had not changed his counsels but had been grievously provoked by the sins of the people. Clarke fixes the guilt on the traffic in the high priesthood, one man ejected for a sum of money and his supplanter outbid by a worse.

Clarke then parts from the rest on the king himself. He takes the king of fierce countenance for the Roman government, since king is often taken for kingdom or empire, and reads the dark sentences as skill in government and its intrigues. The others keep to Antiochus: Ellicott makes the fierce countenance shamelessness and the dark sayings falsehood and dissimulation, Wesley calls him full of subtilty, such as all histories declare him to be, and Calvin says he was notoriously destitute of any nobleness of mind and remarkable for low cunning.

Not by his own power is the hardest clause. Ellicott says not might but cunning will cause his success. Keil and Delitzsch describe the sagacity as cunning in the bad sense, on which ground his deceit succeeds and his heart is lifted up, so that he destroys many not in deep peace but in careless security, and thus unexpectedly. Wesley finds the borrowed strength in the Jewish factions and in the help of Eumenes and Attalus. Clarke, keeping his own reading, says that empire was not strong by virtue of the goat but drew its strength from elsewhere. Calvin canvasses four opinions and settles on none: that the clause compares him with Alexander, that his power was great but unlike his, that his strength lay concealed so that he crept on by clandestine acts rather than open battle, or that it refers to God, who armed him as a scourge. That last sense Calvin calls more profitable and full of useful instruction, yet he fears it is distorted.

The end is not disputed. Calvin will not allow the prince of princes to be the high priest, which he calls too confined and spiritless, but takes it of God, so that the madness of Antiochus proceeded to attacking God himself; and the consolation follows, that he should be broken without hand, divine power sufficing without human aid. Wesley names the affront, the profaning of the temple and the setting up of the image and worship of Jupiter there, and reads the breaking as the disease of which he died. Ellicott says the same shortly, not by the hand of man but by the act of God.
26:
The angel vouches for what he has said, and Gill takes the vouching plainly: the two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings are natural days, to which term the daily sacrifice was to cease and the sanctuary and host be trodden under foot, and then it would be cleansed; the account is clear and plain, with no obscurity in it. Calvin reads it the same way. It is called the vision of the evening and the morning because the angel was treating of the six years and almost a half, and was purposely so expressed lest any one extend it to years or months, as some did; the certainty of the vision rests on this, that God had computed day by day the time of the profanation of the temple until its cleansing. Clarke is the one voice that extends it, reckoning the term at not less than two thousand three hundred years.

Keil and Delitzsch attend to the wording. Because the time was not seen by the prophet but revealed to him in words, they take the clause to refer to what was said, and to depend on the vision rather than on the hours named. They then answer a charge that the confirmation betrays a purpose to make the book falsely appear old: it is much more fitted, they say, to strengthen the weakness of the faithful and console them in the hour of trial.

Why the vision is to be shut up divides them. Ellicott takes the concluding words as comfort to the Jewish Church in her persecution, teaching that God has foreseen her affliction, that it comes from him in his love, and shall last only a short while; this accounts for the firmness of the saints of the Maccabees, and the revelation is kept safe because the time of fulfilment is far off and the comforting words will be needed then. Calvin owns the difficulty: the prophet was instructed in futurity not for his private advantage but for the common usefulness of the people, so a command to keep it obscure seems contrary to his office. His answer is that the greater part would reject the prophecy, and that was no reason to hesitate; it is as if God had deposited a treasure in his hands and said, many may deride thee and think thou art narrating fables, but guard this treasure faithfully.

The sickness is read as sympathy of body with mind. Gill says the afflictions coming upon the people of God and the condition of the temple so affected him that he not only fainted and was struck with a kind of stupor, but had a fit of illness lasting some days, such nearness is there between soul and body. Wesley says he was overwhelmed by a sense of the calamity, and having recovered strength minded his place and trust, and concealed the whole, that they might not see it by his countenance. Calvin denies that the disease happened naturally: it fell upon him because he was suddenly terrified, and where in an ordinary case God did not humble his servant, here he shows the prediction to relate to an event of serious magnitude.

Two last things are inferred from the close. Calvin draws from the king’s business the grievous error of those who think the prophet was in Persia at this period, since he could not return to his duties unless present in the palace; and he warns that the case is rare, asking which of us would be sufficient both for the duties of political government and for those of a pastor and teacher. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the rendering that supplies the first person, that the prophet understood it not, since it rests on giving the command the false sense of concealment; had he been required to keep the prophecy secret, the remark that none understood it would be superfluous.
